1.15.3.en: By this the Shepherd urges His children to a spirit of hope, so He assures the human soul that even if she herself does not know, He knows her perfectly as “the unique in beauty,” since she has become a dwelling for His Holy Spirit, has put on Christ Himself, and been prepared by Him to be His eternal bride.

1.15.4.en: Therefore let the believer examine his depths and realize the new nature that was given to him in Baptism, and let him know that, in the eyes of the heavenly Shepherd, he is beautiful among the whole creation. 2. He also commands her to go forth (“go thy way forth”), for she cannot become “fairest among women” unless she goes forth with her Shepherd outside the camp to bear His reproach (Heb 13:13). Let her go out from the ego or human self, and be crucified with her Bridegroom, so that she lives in Him and by Him, as though He advises her, indeed commands her thus: “If you wish My shepherding, go forth out of yourself and come to My Cross.”

1.15.5.en: In her going forth she goes with the Head Himself, the crucified Shepherd, and with the rest of the members of the body “by the footsteps of the flock,” whether with the holy Fathers who went before or with those who strive. Therefore the Apostle also advises us: “considering the end of their conversation: whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7). If we fear the Cross, let us look at how our holy Fathers went forth to the Cross and were sanctified and adorned. 3. When the soul knows her new position as a beautiful bride and imitates the holy Fathers, bearing the reproach of the Cross outside the camp, that is, outside the human self, she must work... She bears witness to the Shepherd before the kids. Thus she does not live in passivity, but her heart burns for sinners, as the psalmist says: “Dejection hath taken hold upon me because of the sinners that forsake thy law,” so that she may bring them into “the shepherds’ tents,” that is, into the Church of Christ in which the shepherds dwell.

1.16.s.en: A call to struggle and work:

1.16.0.en: Since the Church, being under the shepherding of the Savior Messiah, is bound to bear the responsibility of practical witness to His salvation, bringing the kids into the fold that they may become the sheep of Christ, He asks her to work in the spirit of strength that knows no fear, and the spirit of unity without division, saying to her:

1.16.1.en: “I have compared thee, O my love (my companion), to my horse in Pharaoh’s chariots” [9]. 1. Here we note His calling her “my horse,” in the plural form; for when the soul comes under the shepherding of the Lord Christ and bears the responsibility of witnessing to His Cross, she is bound to work in a spirit of unity with the rest of the horses, working in the one procession of Christ! In her spiritual striving, as in her preaching, she is joined with all the members of the body of Christ, follows in the footsteps of the early Fathers (“go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock”), cares for the generations to come (“feed thy kids”), and joins in the work with those who strive as one of the horsemen in the procession of Christ Jesus our Lord. As though the secret of strength in the believer’s life is that, being joined to Christ the Head of the one Church, he is joined to the whole Church extending from Adam to the end of the ages, working with the rest of the members in one spirit. 2. By calling her “my horse” He declares the Church’s belonging to the Lord Christ. This is the secret of her strength, that she has come to be His possession, acquired by His blood, and He leads her Himself, and she works for the account of His kingdom; therefore St. John the Theologian saw the Church as the white horse of the Lord, “and he that sat on him had a bow; and a crown was given unto him: and he went forth conquering, and to conquer” (Rev 6:2). Every victory of ours is in His name and for His account.

1.16.2.en: And from the Lord’s pride in His Church, which He leads as a horse, He is titled “him that sat on the horse” (Rev 19:19, 21). 3. Horses are distinguished by strength and the ability to enter battles swiftly without fear, for it is said of them: “Hast thou given the horse strength? hast thou clothed his neck with a mane? Canst thou make him leap as a locust?... doth he go out to meet the armed men? He mocketh at fear, and is not affrighted; neither turneth he back from the sword” (Job 39:19-21). And the prophet Zechariah spoke of the strength of the house of Judah thus: “the LORD of hosts hath visited his flock the house of Judah, and hath made them as his goodly horse in the battle” (Zech 10:3). And the Apostle Paul saw himself as one of these horses in the chariot of salvation, so he said: “Thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor 15:57). 4. The horses refer to the heavenly or lofty power of God, for in the book of Habakkuk the prophet says: “His glory covered the heavens... He stood, and measured the earth... Was thy wrath kindled against the rivers, O LORD? was thine anger against the rivers? or thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses, thy chariots of salvation?” (Hab 3-8). And when the servant of Elisha the prophet saw the army surrounding the city he was troubled, but Elisha asked the Lord to open the eyes of the lad, “and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha” (2 Kgs 6:8)... and so on.

1.16.3.en: As for His saying here “in Pharaoh’s chariots,” our Lord affirms that although the believers have become horses of the Lord who carry the heavenly mark, they are “Pharaoh’s chariots,” that is, they live on the earth (in Egypt), and Egypt was known for the excellence of her horses (1 Kgs 10:28-29).

1.16.4.en: Origen sees in the saying “Pharaoh’s chariots” a declaration of her own worthiness to be drowned in the Red Sea, but when she enters the waters of Baptism she comes out pure and holy and becomes a white horse!

1.17.0.en: When the Shepherd had met with His Church and declared to her the truth of her new position, that she is “fairest among women,” and asked her to strive as one of His horses in the chariots of salvation, He began to declare to her the fruit of this work in her life, saying to her:

1.17.1.en: “How beautiful are thy cheeks with rows of jewels (like a dove), and thy neck with chains!

1.17.2.en: We will make thee chains of gold with studs of silver.

1.17.3.en: While the king is in his seat (at his table)” [10-12].

1.17.4.en: We can summarize the fruits of the shepherding in the following: 1. She has the cheeks of a dove, that is, she carries a spirit of humility with chastity. 2. Her neck is adorned with a spirit of obedience and service to others. 3. She enjoys the likeness of gold and studs of silver, that is, the Law and the legislation, until she enjoys gold itself, that is, “the Gospel of grace” or “the heavenly life.”

1.18.0.en: The cheeks of the Church have been adorned with rows of jewels, that is, lines of gems, for she carried within her the Holy Spirit who fills her inner life; this reflected on her face, so it bore the fruit of the Spirit, which is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith and temperance (Gal 5:22).

1.18.1.en: The Septuagint came with “How beautiful are thy cheeks like a dove”... as though the secret of the beauty of the Church’s face is her enjoyment of the fruits of the Holy Spirit who appears in the form of a dove.

1.18.2.en: Origen comments on this text, saying: [He did not say, “How beautiful are thy cheeks,” but says, “How beautiful have thy cheeks become.” He wished to make clear that they were not formerly so beautiful, but this beauty came to her after the Church received the kisses of the Bridegroom, and after He came to her who formerly spoke by the prophets. He cleansed this Church for Himself in the font of water, and made her without spot or wrinkle and gave her to know herself; by this her cheeks became beautiful, for chastity and virtue and virginity—things that she did not have before—have spread in her with a delightful beauty through the Church].

1.18.3.en: The cheek of the dove refers to meekness and purity; as to meekness the Lord instructs us: “Be simple as doves” (Mt 10:16), that is, do not carry the craftiness and cunning of the world; and as to purity, this kind of dove, the Turtle-dove, mentioned in this expression, Origen says has a wonderful nature: if one of the pair dies the other does not accept another in place of the lost one...

1.18.4.en: Origen comments on this text, saying: [The symbol of the Turtle-dove applies to the Church exactly, either because she does not know how to be united with another besides Christ, or because the flight of doves symbolizes chastity and meekness].

1.19.0.en: The neck of man—without adornment—often refers to the coarseness of human nature, but when it is adorned with the gifts of the Holy Spirit it becomes a symbol of spiritual beauty and gentleness in bearing with others... These are the necklaces (the collar or the chain) of the Church! Our neck used to carry shame and disgrace because of our disobedience and pride. But now it carries the yoke of Christ and accepts His obedience, and so it has surpassing spiritual beauty.

1.20.0.en: In the Septuagint it came: “We will make thee a likeness of gold with studs of silver, while the king is at his table.” The Church in the Old Testament had no gold but the likeness of gold and studs of silver, but now that the King has reclined at His table, His bride has “gold.”

1.20.1.en: Since the Lord the King reclined upon His Cross, we have “gold,” that is, “the heavenly life,” after we had formerly been living in the likeness of the heavenly things, “the likeness of gold,” through types and shadows (Gal 3:19; Heb 10:1; 1 Cor 10:11).

1.20.2.en: Some Fathers see that the Church of the Old Testament enjoyed the likeness of gold with studs of silver, that is, enjoyed the Law and the prophets in which the chastity of marriage and widowhood was the rule of life, but when the virgin King came and reclined at His table, He raised in the members of His body the possibility of “the life of virginity,” which is “the law of heaven,” where they neither marry nor are given in marriage.

1.21.0.en: Now that the Bridegroom has likened His Church to His horse in the chariots of salvation, leading her Himself and passing through with her to His kingdom, the Church also looks to Him as a king who fought for her and united with her to raise her up as a queen who sits at His right hand.

1.22.0.en: “While the king reclineth at his table, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof” [12].

1.22.1.en: When our Lord Jesus Christ reigned by the Cross, pouring out His life for her sake, the queen came forward to Him returning love for love, offering her life as pure spikenard, pouring it upon Him, so that its fragrance wafts wherever the Gospel is preached.

1.22.2.en: At the table of the Lord, or His altar, the King meets the queen, and the queen offers the sacrifice of the King Himself, a sweet fragrance acceptable to the Father, and His sacrifice is counted her sacrifice, and His fragrance her spikenard! For all that the King offered on the Cross He offered in the name of the Church and for her account. Therefore the queen, that is the Church, was given to offer the very same sacrifice of His, as the fragrance of the spikenard of the love of the King for the queen and the love of the queen for the King.

1.22.3.en: Thus St. Augustine looks to the sacrifice of the King and sees it as the very sacrifice of the queen, for he says:

1.22.4.en: [You are upon the table! You are within the cup!

1.22.5.en: This is what the Church offers through the mystery of the altar! And as she lifts up the offerings to God she offers herself to Him as an offering!

1.22.6.en: This great, exalted sacrifice is we ourselves!].

1.22.7.en: He says also: [As long as the Church is the body of Him who is the Head, she learns to offer herself (as an offering) through Him].

1.23.0.en: Thus, while the King reclines at His table, the queen gathers with Him, and the fragrance of the knowledge of Him appears in her (2 Cor 2:15), she offers the spikenard of her love to Him, and lays down her life for Him, as He laid down His life for her... so she enters with Him into the myrrh, saying:

1.23.1.en: “A bundle of myrrh is my beloved (my sister’s son) unto me; he shall lie all night betwixt my breasts” [13].

1.23.2.en: If He suffered for her and died, she comes to Him with the myrrh that is used in the anointing oil and in spices... she enters with Him into the tomb carrying myrrh to shroud His body.

1.23.3.en: The queen has realized that her Bridegroom is the King “who conquers death,” whom the tomb cannot hold nor the gates of Hades conceal... she knew Him as “the Resurrection,” the Giver of life, so she prepared for Him myrrh within her so that He might enter into her, into her heart, which became a new tomb... There between her breasts He lodges to enter His holy tomb, where no smell of death is smelled in it, but spikenard and myrrh, and the tomb is changed into a holy temple, in which God declares Himself and dwells.

1.23.4.en: In this call that the queen directs to the King we note the following: 1. The queen does not offer the myrrh in any manner whatever but binds it up and closes it, “a bundle of myrrh,” and as Origen says: [In this way the fragrance of the myrrh is not scattered outside but remains within, so that its fragrance is sweeter and stronger; then the King dwells in her heart, where He finds His rest, and lodges in her bosom]. 2. The queen used the expression “a bundle of myrrh is my beloved unto me” because according to the Law everything not bound or closed is unclean (Num 19:15), and the soul that touches what is unclean is defiled. But Jesus has no blemish at all, but everything in Him is pure and clean... the soul touches Him and is sanctified.

1.23.5.en: Origen sees that the expression “a bundle of a drop of myrrh” refers to the teachings of the Church concerning the divine Incarnation, teachings that bind the truth and gird it so that no heresies seep into it. But the soul that touches heresies—the unbound teachings—becomes unclean. 3. Origen sees that the expression is “a bundle of a drop of myrrh”... for God the Word, the unlimited, became by His Incarnation “like a drop,” emptying Himself, carrying our nature. 4. Origen also sees that the word “my beloved” here is “my brother’s son” or my sister’s son, My Nephew, and since the speaker here is the Church of the Gentiles, the community of the Gentiles represents her elder sister in the knowledge of God, and the Lord Christ came from the Jews according to the flesh, so the queen says “a bundle of a drop of myrrh is my sister’s son unto me,” which refers to the birth of the Lord Christ according to the flesh. 5. The queen did not say “in my heart he lodges” but “between my breasts he lodges,” and perhaps this expression is taken from the ancient custom that the wife hangs on her neck a chain with a miniature picture of her absent husband as a sign of her love and loyalty to him, the picture resting on her chest.

1.23.6.en: And as the King has two breasts, which are “the Old Testament and the New Testament,” by which His Church is nourished, the queen has the same two breasts. For the book of God is the book of the Church, and the Lord rejoices when He finds His Church presenting to the world His word as food for souls. 6. Finally she invites Him to lodge between her breasts, as though she says to Him with the prophet Hosea: “that I put away my whoredoms out of my sight, and my adulteries from between my breasts” (Hos 2:2), so that You find a dwelling in me, O Holy One. Come in and lodge the whole night, for as long as I am in the darkness of this temporal life I need You... Come in until the day of eternity dawns. Lodge between my breasts, for I will hide You, O my God, within me, I will not let You go, for I have no one but You!

1.24.0.en: “A cluster of camphire is my beloved (my sister’s son) unto me in the vineyards of En-gedi” [14].

1.24.1.en: The cluster of camphire is the bundle of henna flowers, on which the bride closes her hand throughout the night before her wedding so that in the morning it becomes red, with a sweet fragrance, and thereby she prepares for her bridegroom; and En-gedi was distinguished for sweet-smelling henna.

1.25.0.en: If the King holds His Cross as the scepter of His kingdom, the queen holds her Bridegroom in her hand and closes upon Him so that His features and the sign of His kingdom are imprinted on her... that is, she bears the color red. She will not be a queen unless she bears the marks of crucifixion and self-giving, and becomes red like her Bridegroom. This is the secret of her strength, and the secret of her wedding and her beauty... Therefore the King addresses her, saying:

1.25.1.en: “Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; thou hast doves’ eyes” [15].

1.26.0.en: For the second time the Bridegroom King enters into dialogue with His bride. The first time He was urging her to know herself and realize that she is “the fairest among women” [8], but now He addresses her affirming to her: “Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair.” And here the word “my love” came “the one near me, My Neighbor,” as though He says to her that the secret of her beauty is her drawing near to Him, after He drew near to her and came down to her. In this St. Ephrem the Syrian says on the night of the feast of the Nativity: [It is a beautiful night, in which He who is beautiful came, and made all beautiful]. As for the King’s repetition of His saying “thou art fair,” it affirms His admiration of her... Here the kingship is mixed with the wedding, and striving with beauty, and esteem and respect with love.

1.27.0.en: 1. The Lord Christ the King sees in the Church a beauty that does not age, whose secret is the dove eyes, for the Holy Spirit—who appears in the form of a dove—has dwelt in her and given her inner enlightenment or spiritual insight.

1.27.1.en: Origen says: [Her eyes are compared to doves surely because she has now come to understand the Holy Scriptures according to the Spirit and not according to the letter. She has come to perceive the spiritual mysteries in the Holy Scriptures, for the dove is a symbol of the Holy Spirit. When we understand the Law and the prophets in a spiritual way we have the dove eyes. Therefore in the book of Psalms a soul longed that she might have the wings of a dove (Ps 55:6), that she might be able to fly to the understanding of spiritual mysteries and settle in the courts of wisdom].

1.27.2.en: Again Origen summarizes the interpretation of this expression, saying: [He says “thine eyes are doves,” seeing and perceiving in a spiritual way].

1.27.3.en: A third time Origen affirms that the eyes of the dove refer to the chaste, pure heart, which can look to the word of God with spiritual understanding, saying: [He who has the eyes of the dove sees the truth and deserves mercy... “The righteous shall see it, and rejoice” (Ps 107:42). Who is this that sees the truth but the one with the chaste, pure look? This does not apply to the bodily eyes but to the eyes of the heart. Enter into the depth, and seek with your spirit other eyes that draw their light from the commandments of God... for the commandment of the Lord is luminous, enlightening the eyes (Ps 118:9). He who has the simple eye can perceive the Spirit descending from heaven in the form of a dove...].

1.27.4.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa also says: [When the pupil of a man’s eye is pure you can behold in them the faces of those looking at them. Thus the beauty of the bride’s eyes is praised because of the image of the dove (the Holy Spirit) that appears in them, for they carry within them an image of what they look to. For the man who no longer looks to flesh and blood, but rather gazes toward the life of the Spirit as the Apostle says, and lives and walks by the Spirit, then by his putting to death the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit he is no longer a natural or carnal man but wholly spiritual. For this reason the Bridegroom praises the soul that has been freed from carnal passions, saying that the image of the dove appears in her eyes, meaning that the impressions of the spiritual life illumine within the purity of the soul]. 2. The dove eyes refer to the simple soul that quickly confesses her sin and comes to the Lord in sincere repentance, as the prophet Ezekiel says: “they shall be like doves, all of them mourning, every one for his iniquity” (Ezek 7:16). 3. The simple eyes refer to simplicity of heart in dealing with others, as the Lord says, “Be simple as doves.” And St. Augustine comments on this divine saying thus: [Note how the doves keep a life of love, for even if they quarrel, in simplicity they do not part from one another]. 4. St. Ambrose says that the Lord Christ always sees His Church as a dove, for He sees her in Baptism putting on the white garment without stain. She shatters all darkness in the waters, and her eyes become doves because the Holy Spirit descends from heaven in the form of a dove. 5. Finally, since the believer’s eyes in Baptism become like doves, his whole life becomes like a dove, for “If thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness” (Mt 6:22-23), so the whole body is enlightened, and man becomes like Noah’s dove which goes forth by the Holy Spirit into the ark, to be always in the bosom of the true Noah!

1.28.0.en: When the soul has dove eyes, looking to the mysteries of God by the Holy Spirit, and perceives the beauty of her Bridegroom, she enters with Him into a deeper union... as she addresses Him, saying:

1.28.1.en: “Behold, thou art fair, my beloved (my sister’s son), yea, pleasant: also our bed is green.

1.28.2.en: The beams (joists) of our house are cedar, and our rafters (the sloping roof) are cypress...” [16].

1.28.3.en: By the Holy Spirit the Church looked to her Bridegroom the King and saw Him truly beautiful in His love and sweet, as though she realized that all the beauty in her goes back to Him. And as Origen says: [It seems that the bride has seen the beauty of her Bridegroom more closely, and perceived with her eyes that were called “doves” the beauty and sweetness of the Word of God. For truly no one can perceive or know the greatness of the sublimity of the Word unless he first receives the eyes of a dove, that is, enjoys spiritual perception].

1.28.4.en: And the fruit of this spiritual perception of the beauty of the King the Bridegroom and the sweetness of His saving works was that she entered with Him into a deeper union, while she is still bound to the body in this world, so she said:

1.28.6.en: What is this bed that is ascribed to the King and the queen (our bed), but the body in which the soul rests, and which receives the indwelling of the Lord in it? For our body is no longer a burden upon the soul nor resisting the work of God, but has been sanctified and has become a temple of the Lord in which our souls rest and in which the Lord rejoices. In it God meets the human soul and through it our souls enjoy fellowship with God, and have the fruit of the Spirit... therefore it is called “green,” that is, fruitful!

1.28.7.en: In this Origen says: [Although the soul is still in the body, she is counted worthy to be in the company of the Word of God... so the divine power extends to give the body goodness, we plant in it the grace of purity and chastity and other good works].

1.28.8.en: The queen does not say “my bed” but “our bed,” for her body is no longer hers alone but belongs to the Bridegroom King; therefore the Apostle Paul called our bodies the members of Christ (1 Cor 6:15). Our bodies have carried a reflection of the inner unity between the divine Word and the soul.

1.28.9.en: And the green bed also declares “the mystery of the Incarnation,” for it is the body of the King, since the divine Word took what is ours... took our humanity, and carried us in Him. Thus we look to His body as a bed for us, since in Him we have rest, and we see in Him our union with Him! The body of the Lord bore fruit—obedience to the Father instead of our disobedience, and purity instead of our impurity, and victory over Satan and all his hosts for our account and in our name, and even worship of the Father in our name, offering new fruits for the account of humanity!

1.29.s.en: The workers in the royal palace:

1.29.0.en: After the queen spoke of the mystery of her union with the King, she declared the responsibility of those working in the royal palace for the account of this unity, so she said:

1.29.1.en: “The beams (joists) of our house are cedar, and our rafters (the sloping roofs) are cypress” [17].

1.29.2.en: Origen sees that the rafters, that is, the sloping roofs which are over the house and which protect it from the heat of the sun and the storms and rains, are the bishops who work in the spirit of Christ and His capacities to preserve the believers, while the beams, that is, the joists through which the whole palace holds together, are the priests who serve for the edification of the children of God. He says: [I think that when the bishops perform their episcopal work faithfully in the Church it is fitting that they be called the rafters that preserve the whole building and protect it from the rains and from the heat of the sun. And I think that next to them in place are the priests who are called the beams].

1.29.3.en: The bishop should be of the cypress tree, for it is distinguished by the following: 1. The cypress tree is known for its great strength and its beautiful fragrance, and as Origen says: [In this is an indication of the bishop’s obligation to have good works and carry the fragrance of the grace of teaching...], that is, he carries two sides: the living Christian spiritual conduct and the ability to teach and spread the sweet fragrance of Christ, serving by his life and by his teaching! 2. Cypress trees are used to signify strength and greatness (2 Kgs 19:23; Isa 14:8), and the shaking of its branches in the wind is compared with the shaking of spears in wars (Nah 2:3). As though the bishop, being a shepherd, must be strong in his spirit and faith, carrying an inner authority by the Holy Spirit and through his holy life. For if he weakens or is disturbed, the flock stumbles and shakes behind him. 3. In the building of Solomon’s temple the floor of the house was covered with boards of cypress (1 Kgs 6:15), as though the bishop, whom the Spirit has set up to be leader, administrator and shepherd of the people, must be humble (spread on the floor of the house), sitting at the feet of his children, washing their feet in a spirit of love full of humility! The people present him as a head who represents the Lord Christ, but in his heart he sees himself in the last rows, showing mercy to the weak and the broken and the despised... He is bound to serve all and not to be served by others. 4. Cypress wood is used in building ships (Ezek 27:5), to cross with them through the sea of this world to the heavenly harbor, and is used to make instruments of music (2 Sam 6:5), to stir in his people the spirit of joy and gladness, and to bestow upon them the spirit of hope in Christ Jesus! 5. Cypress wood is used in making spears (Nah 2:3), since the bishop is bound to keep the faith against every heresy or innovation. 6. Because of its great height the stork chooses it to build its nest in it (Ps 104:7); thus every man—even unbelievers—sees in the spiritual bishop the heart lifted up toward heavenly things and the mind occupied with the eternal things, and finds rest in him in Christ Jesus.

1.29.4.en: And what we have said about the bishop we say also about the priest, for Origen says: [In the same way it was said of the beams that they are of cedar, that the priests may appear full of every virtue of incorruption and have the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ], for cedar is distinguished by its straightness and its sweet fragrance.

1.29.5.en: And cedar was used in making the masts of ships (Ezek 27:5) that they may lead the people to the divine harbor, and in making musical instruments, to stir the spirit of joy in the life of their children. And it was used in making the inner part of Solomon’s temple (1 Kgs 6:20) as in making the altar (1 Kgs 6:18), to teach the priest that his mission is the building of the inner house of the Lord in the heart, so that he does not care for outward show or become occupied with another work, and that he represents the altar, having no work but to carry to his people Christ the Sacrifice and offer on their behalf the offering of prayers. He bears witness to the Cross and does not cease to pray until he brings all into eternal life.
